questions.q: What average annual cost does Gartner's data quality research attribute to poor data quality?
options: Gartner has never studied this
$12.9 million per organization
$500,000 per organization
$1 billion industry-wide total
questions.explain: Gartner's research (cited on its data quality pages, originating from its 2020 data quality market research) puts the average at $12.9 million per year.

questions.q: The lesson says this figure should be treated as what?
options: An order of magnitude / industry average, not a precise number for any one company
An exact number every company will match
A figure that only applies to small businesses
A one-time cost that never recurs
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames it as an industry-average order of magnitude — the real point is that the cost is material and measured, not the exact digit.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five cost categories the lesson lists?
options: Increased office rent
Bad decisions made on bad numbers
Wasted labor reconciling conflicting numbers
Opportunity cost of time spent firefighting data
questions.explain: The five categories are wasted labor, bad decisions, compliance exposure, customer-facing failures, and opportunity cost — office rent isn't one of them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue the real cost is usually higher than any single cited figure?
options: Inflation makes all older statistics invalid
Gartner deliberately underreports its research
Most data-related losses are never traced back to their root cause — an attribution gap
Data quality costs are declining every year
questions.explain: A lost renewal from a billing error gets recorded as 'churn,' not linked back to the data defect — most costs go unattributed entirely.

questions.q: What does the lesson suggest as a practical first step to estimate the cost of poor data at your own organization?
options: Only use the Gartner $12.9 million figure directly as your own cost
Avoid estimating costs since they can never be known
Wait for a formal third-party audit before taking any action
Pick one recurring data problem, estimate hours spent working around it monthly, multiply by a fully-loaded hourly cost
questions.explain: The lesson's suggested approach is a rough but honest estimate — pick one problem, estimate hours, multiply by cost — to get a governance conversation taken seriously.
